cau_hoi: Before entering politics and becoming president of the United States in 1981, what was Ronald Reagan's profession?
giai_thich: Reagan appeared in over 50 Hollywood films and served as president of the Screen Actors Guild. He was the governor of California before serving two terms as president (1981 – 1989). In 1981, he was shot just 69 days after taking office but survived. In 1987 in Berlin, he called on the Soviet leader: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!"

cau_hoi: The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), effective in 1994, includes the United States, Canada, and which country?
giai_thich: NAFTA eliminated most tariffs between the three countries, creating one of the largest free trade areas in the world. Trade between the countries surged, but it also sparked controversy as some factories moved from the U.S. to Mexico. In 2020, NAFTA was replaced by a new agreement called USMCA.

cau_hoi: On September 11, 2001, two towers of the World Trade Center were attacked in which city?
giai_thich: The al-Qaeda terrorist group hijacked four passenger planes. Two crashed into the twin towers in New York, one hit the Pentagon near Washington, and the fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania as passengers fought back against the hijackers. Nearly 3,000 people died. The event led to the war in Afghanistan and changed global aviation security.

cau_hoi: Who is the only person to have held both the office of President of the United States and Chief Justice of the Supreme Court?
giai_thich: William Howard Taft served as president from 1909 to 1913, but his true passion was being a judge. In 1921, President Harding appointed him as Chief Justice, and he remarked that he no longer remembered being president. He was also the first president to throw the ceremonial first pitch of the baseball season, a tradition that continues to this day.

cau_hoi: What number president was Abraham Lincoln of the United States?
giai_thich: Lincoln took office in 1861 and was the first president from the Republican Party. He stood about 1.93 meters tall, making him the tallest president in American history, and often stored papers in his tall hat. He is the only president to have a patent, for a device to lift boats over shoals. His portrait appears on the $5 bill and the 1-cent coin.

cau_hoi: Mount Rushmore, featuring the carved faces of four American presidents, is located in which state?
giai_thich: Sculptor Gutzon Borglum and about 400 workers used dynamite and jackhammers to carve the faces of Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Lincoln, each about 18 meters high. The project was completed from 1927 to 1941 without any worker fatalities. The mountain is sacred to the Lakota people, who believe the land was taken from them unjustly.

cau_hoi: In what year was Brazil's new capital Brasília inaugurated?
giai_thich: President Juscelino Kubitschek aimed to develop the interior region and built the new capital in the highlands in just about 41 months. Architect Oscar Niemeyer and planner Lúcio Costa designed the city to resemble an airplane or a bird when viewed from above. Previously, the capital was Rio de Janeiro. Brasília is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cau_hoi: In what year did the United States hand over full control of the Panama Canal to Panama?
giai_thich: According to treaties signed by U.S. President Jimmy Carter and Panama's leader Omar Torrijos in 1977, the U.S. gradually transferred control of the canal. On December 31, 1999, Panama officially took full management. Since then, Panama has charged tolls for canal passage and expanded the canal with a new set of locks in 2016, allowing larger ships to pass.

cau_hoi: In which country did the Sandinista revolutionary movement, which overthrew dictator Somoza in 1979, operate?
giai_thich: The movement is named after Augusto César Sandino, who led the fight against U.S. Marines occupying Nicaragua from 1927 to 1933. The Somoza family ruled Nicaragua for about 43 years. After 1979, the U.S. supported the 'Contra' forces against the Sandinista government, leading to a conflict that lasted throughout the 1980s.

cau_hoi: Archbishop Óscar Romero, who spoke out for the poor and was assassinated while celebrating Mass in 1980, was in which country?
giai_thich: Romero used radio sermons to denounce violence and injustice in El Salvador, a country on the brink of civil war. On March 24, 1980, he was shot while celebrating Mass in a chapel. His funeral was attended by tens of thousands. In 2018, Pope Francis canonized him. March 24 is International Day for the Right to the Truth.

cau_hoi: In which city did the first Summer Olympics held in Latin America take place in 1968?
giai_thich: The 1968 Mexico Olympics took place at an altitude of about 2,240 meters, where the thin air helped sprinters and long jumpers set records. Bob Beamon jumped 8.90 meters, a record that stood for nearly 23 years. Two African American athletes raised their fists wearing black gloves on the medal podium to protest racism. Rio de Janeiro hosted the Olympics in 2016.

cau_hoi: In which country was the first FIFA World Cup held in 1930?
giai_thich: Uruguay was chosen as the host because it was the Olympic football champion in 1924 and 1928, and because 1930 marked the 100th anniversary of its first constitution. Only 13 teams participated, as many European teams were hesitant about the long sea voyage of about 2 to 3 weeks. Uruguay defeated Argentina 4-2 in the final and became the first champion.

cau_hoi: Which leader of the Haitian revolution was a former slave, later captured by Napoleon and taken to France, where he died in prison in 1803?
giai_thich: Toussaint Louverture learned to read and write despite being born a slave and was a brilliant military strategist. He led the uprising, defeating Spanish and British forces, and became the ruler of Saint-Domingue. In 1802, Napoleon tricked him into negotiations and then arrested him. He died in a cold fortress in the Jura Mountains (France), a year before Haiti's independence.

cau_hoi: "The Cry of Dolores" by priest Miguel Hidalgo on September 16, 1810, marked the beginning of the independence struggle of which country?
giai_thich: In the early hours of September 16, 1810, priest Hidalgo rang the church bell in the village of Dolores and called on the people to rise up against the Spanish government. His army of peasants quickly grew to tens of thousands. In 1811, he was captured and executed. September 16 is Mexico's Independence Day, and each year the President of Mexico repeats the "Cry" from the balcony of the National Palace.

cau_hoi: Which Central American country abolished its army in 1948 and used the budget for education and healthcare?
giai_thich: After a brief civil war in 1948, leader José Figueres declared the army disbanded, and the 1949 constitution officially confirmed this. Costa Rica invested the savings into schools, hospitals, and environmental protection. Today, Costa Rica is one of the most stable democracies in Latin America and is famous for eco-tourism.

cau_hoi: "The Pastry War" of 1838, partly sparked by the vandalism of a bakery in Mexico, was a conflict between Mexico and which country?
giai_thich: A French baker in Mexico claimed that his shop was vandalized by Mexican soldiers. France demanded compensation from Mexico for him and many other French citizens. When Mexico refused, the French fleet blockaded and attacked the port of Veracruz. During the conflict, General Santa Anna lost a leg, and later he held a formal funeral for his leg.

cau_hoi: The American company United Fruit, which had significant political influence in many Central American countries, was famous for growing and exporting which fruit?
giai_thich: In the early 20th century, United Fruit owned vast banana plantations, railroads, and ports in Guatemala, Honduras, and many other countries, and intervened deeply in their politics. The term "banana republic" was coined by writer O. Henry to refer to small countries dominated by a foreign company and local elites. This company is now known as Chiquita.

cau_hoi: "The Boy Heroes" (Niños Héroes) were 6 Mexican cadets who sacrificed themselves in 1847 while defending which castle against American forces?
giai_thich: When American forces attacked Mexico City during the Mexican-American War, military academy students at Chapultepec Castle, some as young as 13 to 19 years old, fought to the end. According to legend, one wrapped the Mexican flag around himself and jumped from the wall so that the Americans could not take the flag. September 13 is a day of remembrance for them in Mexico.

cau_hoi: Hoover Dam, one of the largest construction projects of the Great Depression, was completed in 1936 on which river?
giai_thich: Hoover Dam is approximately 221 meters high, located between Nevada and Arizona, creating Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States. About 21,000 workers labored in temperatures sometimes exceeding 50°C. The project was completed two years ahead of schedule. The dam provides electricity and water to millions of people in Nevada, Arizona, and California, helping the city of Las Vegas to grow.

cau_hoi: Getúlio Vargas, who established the "New State" (Estado Novo) in 1937, was the leader of which country?
giai_thich: Vargas came to power in 1930 through a revolution, then established the Estado Novo dictatorship in 1937. He built industry, established labor laws and minimum wage, earning him the title "Father of the Poor" among workers, but he also suppressed opposition. He was re-elected president in 1950 and committed suicide in 1954 amid a political crisis.

cau_hoi: Which Brazilian emperor tested Alexander Graham Bell's telephone at the Philadelphia exhibition in 1876 and exclaimed, "My God, it works!"?
giai_thich: Pedro II ascended to the throne in 1831 at the age of 5. He was a keen learner, spoke many languages, loved science, astronomy, and photography, and knew scientists like Darwin and Pasteur. He visited the American Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia and stopped by Bell's small booth. His reaction drew attention to Bell's invention.

cau_hoi: Tiradentes, a national hero of Brazil executed in 1792 for plotting independence, had a nickname meaning "tooth puller." What profession did he have?
giai_thich: Joaquim José da Silva Xavier worked in various professions, including tooth pulling, which earned him the nickname Tiradentes. He participated in a plot in Minas Gerais demanding independence from Portugal, partly due to heavy taxes on gold. The plot was betrayed. While others received reduced sentences, he was hanged. April 21 is Tiradentes Day in Brazil.

cau_hoi: Which city was the first capital of Brazil during the colonial period, from 1549 to 1763?
giai_thich: Salvador (Bahia) was established by the Portuguese as the colonial capital in 1549. The city was a center for sugar plantations and the slave trade, so African culture is very prominent here today, such as capoeira and cuisine. In 1763, the capital moved to Rio de Janeiro, near new gold mines. The historic district of Pelourinho in Salvador is a World Heritage Site.

cau_hoi: Why did the Portuguese court move to Brazil in 1808, making Rio de Janeiro the capital of the entire empire?
B: Because the king wanted to travel
D: Because Brazil was richer than Portugal
giai_thich: When the French troops entered Lisbon, about 10,000 – 15,000 people including the royal family, officials, and courtiers boarded ships to flee to Brazil, escorted by the British navy. This was the only time in history that a European monarchy ruled from its colony. Rio was further developed with libraries, schools, and botanical gardens, paving the way for Brazil's independence in 1822.

cau_hoi: Which general commanded the Battle of Ayacucho in 1824, ending Spanish rule in South America?
giai_thich: Sucre was a friend and right-hand man of Bolívar. On December 9, 1824, at Ayacucho (Peru), his forces defeated the last large Spanish army in South America and captured the viceroy. Sucre later became Bolivia's first elected president. He was assassinated in 1830 at the age of 35.

cau_hoi: Which city is the constitutional capital of Bolivia, named after a liberating general?
giai_thich: Bolivia has two capitals: Sucre is the constitutional capital and the location of the Supreme Court, while La Paz is where the government and parliament are located. La Paz is situated at an altitude of about 3,600 meters, making it the highest administrative capital in the world. Sucre, known for its white buildings, is famously called the "White City" and is where Bolivia declared independence in 1825.

cau_hoi: In 1822, Simón Bolívar had a secret meeting in Guayaquil (Ecuador) with which liberating general?
giai_thich: The two greatest "liberators" of South America met in Guayaquil and had a private conversation that went unrecorded. Shortly after the meeting, San Martín unexpectedly withdrew from politics, leaving the liberation of Peru to Bolívar, and then moved to Europe. Historians still debate what the two men discussed.

cau_hoi: The Chaco War (1932 – 1935), the largest conflict in South America in the 20th century, occurred between Bolivia and which country?
giai_thich: The two countries fought over the arid Gran Chaco region, believing it contained oil and because Bolivia wanted access to the sea via the Paraguay River. Many soldiers died from thirst and disease rather than from gunfire. Paraguay won and gained most of the disputed territory. Ironically, oil was not discovered there until 2012.

cau_hoi: In 1990, who became the first elected female president in the Americas?
giai_thich: Violeta Chamorro was the widow of a journalist who opposed the Somoza regime and was assassinated in 1978. In 1990, she unexpectedly defeated the Sandinista faction in the election, ending the war with the Contra forces. Isabel Perón in Argentina served as president from 1974 but was not directly elected to the position. Bachelet, Rousseff, and Kirchner all became presidents later.

cau_hoi: The writer Gabriel García Márquez, author of "One Hundred Years of Solitude" and Nobel Prize in Literature winner in 1982, is from which country?
giai_thich: García Márquez is affectionately called "Gabo" by the people. The novel "One Hundred Years of Solitude" (1967) tells the story of seven generations of the Buendía family in the imaginary town of Macondo, representing the peak of the "magical realism" style, where strange events occur as if they were normal. The book has sold tens of millions of copies. He lived many years in Mexico and passed away there in 2014.

cau_hoi: The poet Pablo Neruda, Nobel Prize in Literature winner in 1971, is from which country?
giai_thich: Pablo Neruda (real name Ricardo Neftalí Reyes) took his pen name from a Czech writer to hide from his father, who did not want him to write poetry. He is one of the most widely read poets of the 20th century and also served as a diplomat. He died in 1973, just 12 days after Pinochet's coup. His house in Isla Negra is filled with collectibles like seashells and prow sculptures.

cau_hoi: The female painter Frida Kahlo, famous for her self-portraits, is from which country?
giai_thich: Frida Kahlo suffered from polio as a child and at 18 had a serious bus accident that left her bedridden for months. During that time, she began painting using a mirror attached to her bed. About 55 of her approximately 140 paintings are self-portraits. She married muralist Diego Rivera. Her "Blue House" in Mexico City is now a museum.

cau_hoi: When did Hugo Chávez begin his presidency in Venezuela?
giai_thich: Hugo Chávez was a military officer who failed in a coup attempt in 1992 and was imprisoned. He won the election in 1998, took office in 1999, and initiated the "Bolivarian Revolution," using oil money for social programs. He remained in power until his death in 2013. Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves in the world.

cau_hoi: Before becoming the president of Brazil, what profession did Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva have?
giai_thich: Lula was born into a poor family in northeastern Brazil, worked as a shoeshiner from a young age, and only completed fifth grade. He worked as a lathe operator in a factory and lost a finger due to a work accident. He led major strikes and founded the Workers' Party. He served two terms as president (2003 – 2010) and was re-elected in 2022.

cau_hoi: In what year did Canada "bring the constitution home," meaning it could amend its constitution without the approval of the British Parliament?
giai_thich: Although Canada had long enjoyed self-governance, amending the constitution still required approval from the British Parliament. In 1982, under Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, the Constitution Act was signed by Queen Elizabeth II in Ottawa, along with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The province of Quebec has yet to officially agree to this constitution.

cau_hoi: In what year did the red and white maple leaf flag of Canada officially become the national flag?
giai_thich: Previously, Canada used a flag that featured the Union Jack in the corner. The debate over a new national flag lasted for many months, known as the "Great Flag Debate," and Parliament reviewed thousands of design proposals. On February 15, 1965, the maple leaf flag was raised for the first time. February 15 is now celebrated as National Flag of Canada Day.

cau_hoi: In what year was the territory of Nunavut in Canada, where the majority of the population is Inuit, established?
giai_thich: Nunavut, meaning "Our Land" in Inuktitut, was separated from the Northwest Territories on April 1, 1999, following the largest land agreement in Canadian history with the Inuit. Nunavut covers about 2 million square kilometers, nearly the size of Mexico, but has only about 40,000 people. The capital, Iqaluit, has no road connections to the rest of Canada.

cau_hoi: How many red and white horizontal stripes are there on the United States flag?
giai_thich: The 13 stripes represent the original 13 colonies that declared independence from Britain, while the 50 stars represent the current 50 states. Each time a new state joins, a star is added. The current flag has been in effect since July 4, 1960, after Hawaii became the 50th state. The 50-star flag design was created by a high school student named Robert Heft for a school project.

cau_hoi: Which British tax act of 1765 sparked a wave of protests with the slogan "No taxation without representation" in the North American colonies?
giai_thich: The Stamp Act required that all printed materials in the colonies, such as newspapers, licenses, and even playing cards, be produced on paper bearing a tax stamp from Britain. Colonists protested vigorously because they had no representation in the British Parliament. They boycotted British goods, and in 1766, Britain had to repeal the act. This was a significant step toward revolution.

cau_hoi: Who wrote the pamphlet "Common Sense" in 1776, calling for the colonists to break away from Britain?
giai_thich: Thomas Paine was an Englishman who had been in America for about a year. The pamphlet, about 47 pages long, was written in simple, easy-to-understand language, arguing that it was absurd for a small island to rule an entire continent. The book sold hundreds of thousands of copies in 1776, compared to a colonial population of about 2.5 million. Washington had it read to his soldiers.

cau_hoi: Which two former U.S. presidents signed the Declaration of Independence and died on July 4, 1826, exactly 50 years after the Declaration?
giai_thich: Jefferson and Adams were once close friends, then became political rivals, and reconciled in old age through hundreds of letters. Jefferson died a few hours earlier in Virginia. Adams, in Massachusetts, is said to have uttered his last words, "Jefferson still lives," unaware that his friend had just passed away. James Monroe also died on July 4, 1831.

cau_hoi: The famous "Liberty Bell" with its large crack is displayed in which city?
giai_thich: The bell was cast in London in 1752 for the building where the Declaration of Independence was later signed. It cracked on its first test, was recast, and the large crack we see today appeared in the 19th century. The inscription on the bell calls for "proclaiming liberty throughout all the land." Abolitionists adopted the bell as a symbol and named it the "Liberty Bell."

cau_hoi: Susan B. Anthony is famous for her fight for what rights in 19th century America?
giai_thich: In 1872, Susan B. Anthony was arrested for daring to vote in the presidential election and was fined $100, but she never paid the fine. She traveled across America giving speeches for over 50 years. She died in 1906, 14 years before American women gained the right to vote. The 19th Amendment is sometimes referred to as the "Susan B. Anthony Amendment."

cau_hoi: Who is the person depicted on the $10 bill despite never having been president?
giai_thich: Alexander Hamilton was born in the Caribbean, orphaned at a young age, moved to New York to study, and became an aide-de-camp to Washington. He was the first Secretary of the Treasury, established the national bank, and the financial system of the United States. He died in 1804 after a duel with Vice President Aaron Burr. His life is the subject of the famous musical 'Hamilton.' Franklin appears on the $100 bill, and he was also not a president.

cau_hoi: The Erie Canal, completed in 1825, connects the Great Lakes with which river to allow ships to reach New York Harbor?
giai_thich: The Erie Canal is approximately 584 km long, mostly dug by human and horse power, with 83 locks. The cost of transporting goods from the West to the East Coast was reduced by about 90%. Thanks to the canal, New York became the largest port city in the United States. Many mocked the project as 'Clinton's Ditch,' named after Governor DeWitt Clinton.

cau_hoi: How long did the famous Pony Express mail service operate in the American West?
giai_thich: The Pony Express operated from April 1860 to October 1861, delivering mail approximately 3,000 km from Missouri to California in just about 10 days. Young, lightweight riders changed horses at stations spaced about 16 to 24 km apart. The service ended just two days after the completion of the transcontinental telegraph line. Despite its short existence, it became a legend of the West.

cau_hoi: Which great fire in 1871 destroyed much of the downtown area of a major American city, leaving about 100,000 people homeless?
giai_thich: The fire started on the evening of October 8, 1871, near the O'Leary family's barn. Legend has it that a cow knocked over a lantern, but this story was likely fabricated by a journalist. Due to wooden buildings and a dry summer, the fire raged for about 2 days. Chicago was quickly rebuilt, and it was here that the world's first skyscraper was built in 1885.

cau_hoi: The ancient Tiwanaku civilization, which was a major religious and political center in the Andes, developed near which lake?
giai_thich: Tiwanaku developed around 500 – 1000 AD at an altitude of nearly 3,850 meters, now part of Bolivia. The Tiwanaku people built the Sun Gate carved from a single stone and created floating farms with water channels to keep crops warm from frost. The Incas later regarded Lake Titicaca as the origin of the world. It is the highest navigable lake in the world.

cau_hoi: In 1903, Brazil purchased the Acre region, rich in rubber trees, from which country?
giai_thich: During the rubber boom, tens of thousands of Brazilians migrated to the Acre region of Bolivia to harvest rubber sap. After conflicts, according to the 1903 Treaty of Petrópolis, Bolivia ceded Acre to Brazil in exchange for money and a promise to build the Madeira-Mamoré railway. This railway had thousands of workers die during its construction, hence it was called 'the Devil's railway.'

cau_hoi: The city of Chan Chan, the largest pre-Columbian city in America built of adobe bricks, was the capital of which civilization?
giai_thich: The Chimú ruled the northern coast of Peru from about 900 to 1470, before being conquered by the Incas. Chan Chan covers about 20 km², with mud walls up to 9 meters high decorated with patterns of fish, birds, and ocean waves. Due to being made of mud, the city is threatened by heavy rains from the El Niño phenomenon and is on the list of World Heritage sites at risk.

cau_hoi: The tomb of the 'Lord of Sipán,' filled with gold and silver artifacts, discovered in Peru in 1987, belonged to which civilization?
giai_thich: The Moche lived on the northern coast of Peru from about 100 to 800 AD. In 1987, archaeologists discovered the tomb of a lord that had never been looted, filled with jewelry made of gold, silver, and precious stones. This discovery has been compared to the tomb of Tutankhamun in Egypt. The Moche were also famous for their vividly realistic portrait pottery.

cau_hoi: The city of Caral, considered one of the oldest cities in America (around 2600 BC), is located in which country?
giai_thich: Caral features step pyramids and circular plazas, built around the same time as the Egyptian pyramids. Notably, archaeologists have found almost no weapons or signs of warfare here. The people of Caral used quipu and played various flutes made from bird bones. Caral is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

cau_hoi: Which indigenous people in southern Chile successfully resisted the Spanish for about 300 years?
giai_thich: The Mapuche fought bravely and learned to use the horses of the Spanish. In 1553, they killed Governor Pedro de Valdivia, who founded the city of Santiago. Spain had to accept the Biobío River as a border and signed many treaties with them. The Mapuche were only conquered by the Chilean and Argentine states at the end of the 19th century.

cau_hoi: The Inca referred to their empire as "Tawantinsuyu." What does this name mean?
giai_thich: The empire was divided into four large regions (suyu), meeting at the capital Cusco, which was considered the center of the world. Each region had its own governor, and roads radiated from Cusco in four directions. The Incas believed that the emperor was the son of the Sun God Inti, so "Land of the Sun" is a misleading option.

cau_hoi: The Amazon River was named by explorer Francisco de Orellana in 1542 based on which Greek legend?
giai_thich: Orellana was the first European to navigate the entire length of the Amazon River, taking about 8 months from the Andes to the Atlantic Ocean. His crew reported fighting against warriors they believed were women, leading them to think of the Amazon warrior women from Greek mythology. The Amazon River has the largest water flow in the world, accounting for about 20% of the river water that flows into the oceans.

cau_hoi: The legend of "El Dorado" (The Gilded Man) originated from the rituals of the Muisca people in which modern-day country?
giai_thich: The Muisca had a ritual when a new leader ascended: he was covered in gold dust and then went out on a raft to the middle of Lake Guatavita, throwing gold objects into the water as offerings to the gods. The story was exaggerated into a city of gold, leading many European explorers to their demise in search of it. The Muisca gold raft is now in the Gold Museum in Bogotá.

cau_hoi: Cerro Rico in Potosí, the largest silver mine in the world during the Spanish colonial period, is located in which country?
giai_thich: Since 1545, Spain extracted vast amounts of silver from Potosí, making it one of the largest and richest cities in the world in the 17th century. Indigenous people were forced to work in the mines under extremely harsh conditions, with hundreds of thousands dying. In Spanish, "worth like Potosí" means extremely wealthy.

cau_hoi: The Manila galleon ships (1565 – 1815) connected Acapulco in Mexico with the city of Manila in which country?
giai_thich: Each year, one or two large ships crossed the Pacific, carrying silver from the Americas to Manila to purchase silk, porcelain, and spices from China and Asia. The journey from Manila to Acapulco could take 4 to 6 months. This is considered the first true global trade route, connecting Asia, the Americas, and Europe. As a result, items like mangoes and chili peppers were also exchanged between the two shores of the Pacific.

cau_hoi: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, a 17th-century nun known as "The Tenth Muse," was a famous poet from which country?
giai_thich: Sor Juana was a prodigy, able to read at the age of 3 and once wanted to disguise herself as a boy to attend university. She entered a convent partly to have time to study and had a personal library of about 4,000 books. She wrote poetry, plays, and a famous letter defending women's right to education. Her portrait appears on the 200 peso bill in Mexico.

cau_hoi: In 1755, the British expelled the Acadians (of French origin) from Nova Scotia. Many of them settled in Louisiana and became which community?
giai_thich: During the "Great Expulsion," about 10,000 Acadians were forced onto ships, with families being separated. Many later arrived in Louisiana, which was then under Spanish rule, where French was spoken. The term "Acadian" gradually evolved into "Cajun." Cajuns are famous for their spicy cuisine like jambalaya and gumbo, and for their music featuring the accordion.

cau_hoi: William Penn, a Quaker, established which colony in North America in 1681?
giai_thich: King Charles II owed William Penn's father a large sum of money, so he repaid it with a large tract of land in North America. The name Pennsylvania means "Penn's Woods." Penn founded the colony with religious freedom and signed a peace treaty with the Lenape Native Americans. He designed the city of Philadelphia, which means "City of Brotherly Love."

cau_hoi: The colony of Maryland was established in 1634 primarily as a refuge for which religious group that faced discrimination in England?
giai_thich: Lord Baltimore (the Calvert family), a Catholic, founded Maryland so that Catholics could live and worship freely, as they were restricted in England. In 1649, Maryland passed the Toleration Act, one of the first laws in America protecting religious freedom for Christians. The city of Baltimore was named after this family.

cau_hoi: Roger Williams established the colony of Rhode Island in 1636 after being expelled from Massachusetts for what reason?
A: He advocated for religious freedom and the separation of church and state
giai_thich: Roger Williams was a minister who believed that the government should not impose religious beliefs on the people and that land should be purchased fairly from the Native Americans. Expelled in the winter, he was helped by the Narragansett people. He founded the settlement of Providence ("God's Favor"), where people of all religions, including Jews and Quakers, were accepted.

cau_hoi: The Treaty of Ghent, signed in December 1814, ended which war?
D: War of 1812 between the U.S. and Britain
giai_thich: The treaty was signed in the city of Ghent (now in Belgium). According to the treaty, everything returned to the status quo ante bellum, with neither side losing or gaining territory. Nevertheless, Americans viewed the war as a 'second war of independence,' while Canadians took pride in having repelled American invasions. The war helped shape national identities in both countries.

cau_hoi: Which battle in the U.S. in 1815 occurred after the peace treaty ending the war was signed, but the news had not yet reached the location?
giai_thich: On January 8, 1815, American forces led by General Andrew Jackson defeated the British in New Orleans, inflicting around 2,000 casualties on the British while suffering only about 70 American casualties. The Treaty of Ghent had been signed on December 24, 1814, but at that time, news had to travel by sailing ship across the Atlantic, taking weeks. The victory helped Jackson later become president.

cau_hoi: Shawnee leader Tecumseh, who sought to establish a large alliance of Native peoples, allied with which country during the War of 1812?
giai_thich: Tecumseh traveled widely calling for Native peoples to unite against American encroachment. During the War of 1812, he allied with the British and helped capture Fort Detroit. In 1813, he was killed in the Battle of the Thames in Canada. After his death, the dream of a large Native alliance shattered.

cau_hoi: Which trail, approximately 3,200 km long, brought hundreds of thousands of settlers by wagon from Missouri to the Pacific Coast in the mid-19th century?
giai_thich: From the 1840s, families sold their possessions, bought covered wagons, and traveled for about 4 to 6 months across plains, mountains, and rivers to reach the fertile lands of Oregon. About 1 in 10 people died on the journey, mostly from cholera. Wagon wheel ruts can still be seen in some places. There is even a famous educational computer game called 'The Oregon Trail.'

cau_hoi: In 1847, the Mormon followers led by Brigham Young established which city in the western United States?
giai_thich: Persecuted in the East, the Mormons moved west in search of a place where they could live freely. Upon reaching the valley near the Great Salt Lake in Utah, Brigham Young is said to have declared, 'This is the place.' They built an irrigation system that transformed the arid land into arable land. Salt Lake City is now the capital of Utah and the headquarters of the Mormon Church.

cau_hoi: Which record does U.S. President William Henry Harrison hold?
A: Shortest time in office, only 31 days
giai_thich: In 1841, Harrison, then 68 years old, delivered the longest inaugural address in history, nearly 2 hours long, in cold and rain, without wearing a coat or hat. A few weeks later, he fell ill and died just 31 days into his term. He was the first president to die in office. His grandson, Benjamin Harrison, later also became president.

cau_hoi: According to the Homestead Act of 1862, how much land could settlers in the western U.S. receive for free if they farmed it for 5 years?
giai_thich: Anyone, including women, immigrants, and later former slaves, could apply for land if they built a house and farmed it for 5 years. About 1.6 million people received land under this act, totaling about 10% of the land area of the U.S. However, most of this land was originally taken from Native peoples.

cau_hoi: What event does Juneteenth (June 19) in the U.S. commemorate?
A: The day the last enslaved people in Texas were informed of their freedom in 1865
B: The day World War II ended
C: The day the Declaration of Independence was signed
D: The day women gained the right to vote
giai_thich: Although the Emancipation Proclamation had been in effect since 1863, many enslaved people in Texas, the farthest region of the South, were not aware. On June 19, 1865, General Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston and announced that all enslaved people were free, liberating about 250,000 individuals. Since 2021, Juneteenth has become a federal holiday in the U.S.

cau_hoi: Which event in 1890 in South Dakota, when U.S. troops killed hundreds of Lakota people, is often regarded as the end of the wars with Native peoples in the U.S.?
giai_thich: On December 29, 1890, when soldiers disarmed a group of Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek, a shot was fired, and soldiers opened fire, killing about 250-300 people, many of whom were women and children. The event occurred amid the spread of the religious movement 'Ghost Dance.' In 1973, Native activists occupied Wounded Knee for 71 days to demand rights.

cau_hoi: Which tribe did Chief Joseph, who famously said 'From now on, I will fight no more forever,' belong to?
giai_thich: In 1877, when forced to leave their homeland in Oregon, Chief Joseph led about 700 Nez Perce people, mostly women, children, and the elderly, fleeing approximately 1,900 km toward Canada. They defeated U.S. troops multiple times. Just 60 km from the Canadian border, they were surrounded, and Joseph surrendered with an emotional speech.

cau_hoi: In 1853, why did the U.S. purchase the Gadsden Purchase from Mexico?
giai_thich: The Gadsden Purchase, now part of southern Arizona and New Mexico, covers about 77,000 square kilometers and was bought for $10 million. This flat land was suitable for building a southern transcontinental railroad. It was the last territorial expansion of the U.S. on the mainland (excluding Alaska). The city of Tucson is located in this area.

cau_hoi: Who was the U.S. Secretary of State that negotiated the purchase of Alaska in 1867, which was mocked as "his folly"?
giai_thich: William Seward was Lincoln's Secretary of State and was severely injured on the same night Lincoln was assassinated when a conspirator attacked him at home. When he purchased Alaska, the press called it "Seward's Folly" and Alaska "Seward's Icebox." Later, Alaska became very valuable due to gold, fish, and oil. The state of Alaska has a holiday called "Seward's Day" in March.

cau_hoi: Who is the only U.S. president not affiliated with any political party?
giai_thich: Washington feared that political parties would divide the nation. In his farewell address in 1796, he warned Americans about the dangers of partisan spirit. However, even in his government, Hamilton and Jefferson formed opposing factions, becoming the first parties. Washington is also the only president to be elected by the Electoral College with 100% of the votes.

cau_hoi: Which U.S. president served in the House of Representatives for 17 years after leaving the White House, fighting against slavery?
giai_thich: John Quincy Adams was the son of President John Adams and served as the 6th president (1825 – 1829). After losing the election, he was elected to the House of Representatives, where he persistently opposed the "gag rule" that prohibited discussions on slavery. He also successfully defended the Africans who revolted on the Amistad ship. He collapsed in the House in 1848.

cau_hoi: What was the significance of the Supreme Court's ruling in Marbury v. Madison in 1803?
A: Established the court's power to declare a law unconstitutional
C: Established Washington D.C. as the capital
D: Allowed the purchase of the Louisiana Territory
giai_thich: Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that a portion of a law passed by Congress was contrary to the Constitution and thus invalid. From then on, U.S. courts had the power to "review the constitutionality" of laws, placing the judiciary on par with Congress and the President. This is one of the most important rulings in American history.

cau_hoi: What issue sparked the violent "Bleeding Kansas" period in the 1850s?
C: Whether to allow slavery in the Kansas territory
giai_thich: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 allowed people in the new territory to vote on the issue of slavery. Pro-slavery and anti-slavery supporters flooded into Kansas, establishing two rival governments and killing each other. About 55 people died. This is considered a "dress rehearsal" for the American Civil War.

cau_hoi: In 1859, where did abolitionist John Brown attack a federal armory, hoping to spark a slave uprising?
giai_thich: John Brown and 21 men, including his sons, seized the armory at Harpers Ferry. However, no uprising occurred, and the army led by Robert E. Lee captured him. He was executed for treason. The North viewed him as a martyr, while the South saw him as a terrorist, deepening the divide between the two regions.

cau_hoi: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 was the first law in the U.S. to prohibit immigration from which nationality?
giai_thich: Many Chinese workers came to the U.S. during the gold rush and built the transcontinental railroad. During economic hardship, they were blamed for taking jobs. The 1882 law prohibited Chinese laborers from immigrating and lasted until 1943. This was the first law in U.S. history to ban immigration based on nationality. In 2012, the U.S. Congress officially expressed regret for this law.

cau_hoi: Booker T. Washington, a former slave who became a famous educator, founded which school in 1881?
giai_thich: Booker T. Washington advocated that African Americans should learn trades and become economically self-sufficient before demanding political rights. The Tuskegee Institute in Alabama was built by the students themselves. Scientist George Washington Carver taught here, researching hundreds of uses for the peanut. During World War II, famous black pilots were trained at Tuskegee.

cau_hoi: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), the oldest civil rights organization in the U.S., was founded in what year?
giai_thich: The NAACP was founded in 1909 by a group of black and white individuals, including scholar W. E. B. Du Bois, the first black person to earn a Ph.D. from Harvard University. The organization focused on legal battles, such as the Brown case in 1954, and campaigning against racial violence. Rosa Parks was once the secretary of the NAACP in Montgomery.

cau_hoi: In which decade did the Harlem Renaissance of African Americans in New York flourish?
giai_thich: In the 1920s, Harlem in New York became the center of African American art, literature, and music. Notable figures included poet Langston Hughes, writer Zora Neale Hurston, and musician Duke Ellington. Jazz thrived in the clubs here. The movement helped affirm the pride and identity of Black Americans.

cau_hoi: In 1947, Jackie Robinson became the first Black player to compete in which major professional sport in modern America?
giai_thich: Jackie Robinson took the field for the Brooklyn Dodgers on April 15, 1947, breaking the color barrier in Major League Baseball. He endured abuse and threats but vowed not to retaliate. He won the Rookie of the Year award that year. Every April 15, all Major League players wear his number 42.

cau_hoi: The Scopes Trial in 1925 in Tennessee, also known as the "Monkey Trial," prosecuted a teacher for teaching students about what?
giai_thich: Tennessee had a law prohibiting the teaching that humans evolved from other animals. Teacher John Scopes agreed to be tried to challenge this law. The trial was broadcast nationwide on the radio, with two famous lawyers debating fiercely. Scopes was fined $100, but the verdict was later overturned due to a procedural error. The law was not repealed until 1967.

cau_hoi: In 1927, who became the first person to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic Ocean from New York to Paris?
giai_thich: Charles Lindbergh, 25 years old, flew the single-engine plane "Spirit of St. Louis" for about 33.5 hours without sleep, carrying extra fuel tanks that required him to use a periscope to see ahead. About 150,000 people welcomed him at Le Bourget Airport in Paris. He received a $25,000 prize and became the most famous person in the world at that time.

cau_hoi: The famous aviator Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while attempting to fly around the world in which year?
giai_thich: In 1932, Earhart became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. In 1937, along with navigator Fred Noonan, she attempted to fly around the world along the equator. After covering about two-thirds of the journey, her plane disappeared near Howland Island. Despite a large search effort, she was never found, and this remains a major mystery.

cau_hoi: The "Dust Bowl" disaster in the 1930s, when massive dust storms devastated farms, occurred in which region of the United States?
giai_thich: Farmers plowed up natural grasslands to plant wheat, breaking the root systems that held the soil. When a prolonged drought occurred, winds blew the topsoil into massive black dust clouds, sometimes reaching as far as Washington and New York. About 2.5 million people were forced to leave their homes. John Steinbeck's novel "The Grapes of Wrath" tells their story.

cau_hoi: The Bretton Woods Conference in 1944 established which international financial organizations?
C: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank
giai_thich: In July 1944, while World War II was still ongoing, representatives from 44 countries met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to construct a post-war financial system. The conference established the IMF and the World Bank, and pegged the value of currencies to the U.S. dollar. British economist John Maynard Keynes was a key figure.

cau_hoi: "The Truman Doctrine" of 1947 was initially proposed to assist which two countries against the influence of communism?
giai_thich: When Britain announced it could no longer afford to support Greece, which was in a civil war, and Turkey, President Truman proposed that Congress provide $400 million in aid to these countries. He declared that the U.S. would support free peoples resisting external pressures. This doctrine marked the U.S. policy of "containment" during the Cold War.

cau_hoi: The Organization of American States (OAS) was established in 1948 in which city?
giai_thich: The OAS Charter was signed by 21 countries in Bogotá, Colombia, in April 1948. At that time, the famous political leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán was assassinated, causing a major riot in the capital known as "Bogotazo." Today, the OAS has 35 member states, and its headquarters is located in Washington, which can lead to confusion.

cau_hoi: In 1954, a CIA-backed coup overthrew the elected president Jacobo Árbenz of which country?
giai_thich: President Árbenz implemented land reforms, redistributing the unused land of the United Fruit Company to farmers. The U.S. believed he was communist-leaning, and the CIA organized a coup operation codenamed PBSuccess. After the coup, Guatemala fell into a series of military governments and a civil war that lasted 36 years (1960 – 1996). In 2011, the Guatemalan government officially apologized to the Árbenz family.

cau_hoi: The "Alliance for Progress" program proposed by President Kennedy in 1961 aimed to assist which region?
giai_thich: After the Cuban Revolution, the U.S. was concerned that Latin American countries would follow a similar path. Kennedy proposed an aid program of about $20 billion over 10 years to promote education, healthcare, housing, and land reform. However, the results were not as expected, and during that decade, many Latin American countries fell into military coups.

cau_hoi: In 1983, the U.S. sent troops to which small Caribbean island nation after a coup there?
giai_thich: After Prime Minister Maurice Bishop was overthrown and killed by the far-left faction in the government, President Reagan ordered troops to Grenada, citing the need to protect about 600 American medical students and to prevent Cuban influence. The operation, named "Urgent Fury," ended within a few days. Grenada is famous for its nutmeg, which is depicted on its national flag.

cau_hoi: In 1989, U.S. forces attacked Panama to capture which leader?
giai_thich: Manuel Noriega was a former CIA collaborator but was later accused by the U.S. of drug trafficking. In December 1989, the U.S. launched Operation "Just Cause" with about 27,000 troops. Noriega sought refuge in the Vatican embassy, and U.S. forces played loud rock music outside for several days. He finally surrendered in early January 1990 and was brought to the U.S. for trial.

cau_hoi: The 1992 United Nations Earth Summit on environment and development was held in which city?
giai_thich: The summit had participation from about 170 countries, with over 100 heads of state. Countries signed the Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Convention on Biological Diversity. A 12-year-old Canadian girl, Severn Cullis-Suzuki, delivered a famous speech known as "The Speech that Silenced the World for 6 Minutes." Kyoto (1997) and Paris (2015) were later venues for climate agreements.

cau_hoi: On January 1, 1994, the same day NAFTA took effect, the Zapatista movement (EZLN) rose up in which Mexican state?
giai_thich: The movement primarily consisted of Maya farmers in Chiapas, the poorest state in Mexico, named after Emiliano Zapata. They protested the neglect of indigenous people and feared that NAFTA would bankrupt corn farmers. Their spokesperson, "Subcomandante Marcos," always wore a ski mask and smoked a pipe. The movement became famous for using the internet to garner international support.

cau_hoi: In 2016, the Colombian government signed a peace agreement to end more than 50 years of conflict with which armed group?
giai_thich: FARC (Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia) began operations in 1964. The conflict resulted in about 220,000 deaths and millions displaced. After four years of negotiations in Cuba, both sides signed an agreement. President Juan Manuel Santos received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2016. FARC disarmed and transformed into a political party.

cau_hoi: The United States severed diplomatic relations with Cuba in which year, before the two countries reopened embassies in 2015?
giai_thich: In January 1961, just weeks before President Eisenhower left office, the U.S. cut diplomatic ties with Cuba after Castro's government nationalized American companies. The U.S. also imposed an economic embargo that continues to this day. In 2015, under President Obama, the two countries reopened embassies after 54 years. In 2016, Obama became the first sitting U.S. president to visit Cuba in 88 years.

cau_hoi: Which American adventurer declared himself president of Nicaragua in 1856?
giai_thich: William Walker was a doctor, lawyer, and journalist who led a group of mercenaries to Nicaragua, exploiting the civil war there to seize power. He declared himself president, made English the official language, and reinstated slavery. Central American countries united to expel him. In 1860, he was captured and executed by firing squad in Honduras. Nicaragua commemorates the victory over Walker annually.

cau_hoi: "The Football War" in 1969, which erupted after World Cup qualifying matches, was a conflict between El Salvador and which country?
giai_thich: The underlying causes were land tensions and Honduras' expulsion of tens of thousands of immigrants from El Salvador. The World Cup qualifying matches in 1970 between the two countries, along with fan riots, added fuel to the fire. The war lasted only about 100 hours but resulted in approximately 3,000 deaths. Polish journalist Ryszard Kapuściński named it this.

cau_hoi: The political agreement of 1877 (Compromise of 1877) in the U.S. resolved the controversial presidential election by withdrawing all federal troops from the South, officially ending which historical period?
giai_thich: After the closely contested presidential election of 1876 between Rutherford B. Hayes and Samuel Tilden, the two parties reached a secret compromise allowing Hayes to take office on the condition that all federal troops be withdrawn from Southern states. This move ended the post-Civil War Reconstruction Era, leaving Black people in the South without military protection and leading to the establishment of Jim Crow segregation laws that lasted for decades.
